Where this goes wrong in practice

retrofit first, rip-and-replace never fails, when it fails, in one specific place: the demo gap: pilots on curated feeds, production on messy reality — and a twin that drifts from the asset until operators stop opening it.

Against retrofit first, rip-and-replace never, the strongest counter-case is worth naming: the twin-first thesis can produce beautiful models of assets nobody needed simulated. The twin earns its keep on the decisions it changes, not the fidelity it displays.
The practice, as we run it

In delivery, retrofit first, rip-and-replace never becomes a specific discipline: we connect machines, fleets and facilities into one operational picture, then close the loop into maintenance, scheduling and control. Every program in the IoT, Twin & Robotics domain carries the same obligations — a signed baseline, named gate criteria, and evidence generated by running the system rather than preparing for a meeting.
Start with the diagnostic, not the contract: retrofit first, rip-and-replace never baselined in two weeks, and a scoped proposal only if the delta justifies it.
